newsitem.title: UK: Sugar-Slack raws activity before Brazilian exports.
newsitem.headline: Sugar-Slack raws activity before Brazilian exports.

text.p: Physical sugar brokers reported little activity in the second-hand raws market this week as Brazil's new crop has yet to come on stream and Cuba holds back cargoes in the hope of better prices.
The other principal factor in the supply equation is Thailand, which hopes to sell to China later in the year but still has low prices for nearby shipment.
"It's really quiet...there's very little in the way of sugar being talked about," said one broker.
"There's very little demand for nearby, that's why the premiums are so low on Thais. They've got lowish prices for May/July because they'd like to get rid of some," he said.
May/July premiums were quoted at 28/35 points bid/offer, while July/September sugars were quoted at 55/65 points to reflect the expected demand from China.

More than half of Thailand's cane crushing mills have closed operations for the season, which normally ends in May or June. Industry sources have said the season might end earlier than anticipated due to lower cane output.

Cuba, which has been shipping bulk raws at a steady rate since January, is thought to be keeping back at least a few cargoes to satisfy demand before Brazil's centre-south returns as an exporter in late May or June.
Sellers of second-hand Cuban raws are reported to be scarce, with bids quoted at around 30 points discount to New York futures and up from 35 points last week.
"There is the odd buyer of Cubans around but I think only to take into his book because it's probably the cheapest raw sugar around," the broker said.
Other traders dismissed market talk that the amount of sugar remaining in Cuba was substantial but agreed that more would definitely emerge in the coming weeks.
"I think this assertion that there's still a huge amount of sugar still to come out of Cuba is probably wrong," said one physical trader.
"But I think there probably is still some to come -- it's just when and if the Cubans want to let it go."
Although most export contracts had already been signed for this year, and shipments had run smoothly, it was still unknown when the crop would end, he said.
"There has been a very healthy amount of sugar exported from the country...but in essence they are seeing what they can get for it now," he said.

Russia has been a significant raws importer during last week but its Black Sea port of Novorossisk is now congested as some five vessels wait offshore loaded with around 140,000 tonnes. Some ships have diverted to Riga.

Several sugar traders in London and Moscow have said between 50,000 and 150,000 tonnes of raws, the bulk of which was likely to be Cuban, should be delivered to Russia soon. Some said the total could be even higher.
Russia's high internal price for white sugar could also be encouraging tolling operations, they added.
In Brazil, raw sugar cargoes from the centre-south were quoted at a premium of 30 points over New York's July contract as a notional value for June/July shipment.
But traders said bids and offers for raw sugar were scarce and there was also little interest in the lower-quality white sugars such as 100 and 150 ICUMSA.

The main talking point with Brazil at the moment is the amount of raw sugar remaining in the country's other sugar-producing area, the north north-east, some of which could be delivered against New York's May expiry.
Some have estimated the quantity to be as much as 180,000 tonnes, although a portion of this will have been earmarked to be shipped to the U.S. under quota and more will go for re-export.
"There is talk of quite a large quantity of raws still in the north which may be delivered against the tape," (futures expiry) said another trader.
Central American producers such as Mexico, Guatemala and Nicaragua were likely to feature as delivered origins, he said.
